claims.text: The initially solid nanoparticles contain Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu in near-equimolar ratios.
The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles nominally have a single solid-solution phase.
Copper is the lower-melting-point element in the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu system.
Early surface or microstructural segregation of Cu governs the onset and progression of premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Cu-enriched nanoscale regions require less thermal energy to melt than chemically uniform regions.
Annealing or synthesis treatments can be used to create otherwise comparable nanoparticles with either maximized chemical uniformity or mild Cu segregation.
Extended high-temperature annealing will maximize chemical uniformity in the baseline Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Localized Cu-enriched regions or clusters act as nucleation sites for melting.
Segregation lowers local cohesive energy and thereby lowers local melting barriers.
Segregated regions nucleate melting at lower temperatures and broaden the premelting regime relative to a uniformly mixed particle.
Chemically heterogeneous nanoparticles will exhibit an earlier premelting onset and a more gradual melting transition than chemically uniform baseline particles.
Chemically uniform baseline particles will exhibit a delayed and sharper melting transition.
The proposed comparison holds heating conditions constant while varying elemental homogeneity.
The hypothesis is restricted to the premelting-to-melting temperature regime and excludes particles undergoing additional phase transformations.
The magnitude of the melting-onset shift and transition-width change may depend on particle size, segregation extent, and measurement sensitivity.
A lack of a statistically significant difference in either premelting onset temperature or melting-transition width between homogenized and segregated groups would falsify the hypothesis.
